prompt: In the textbook page-I/O model, R has 2,000 pages and S has 400 pages. At first memory is too small to hold S, so the join runs as a Grace hash join. Then the join is given enough memory to hold all of S and its hash table. What happens to the page I/O, ignoring output writes?

options.text: Nothing changes: a hash join always partitions both inputs first
options.explanation: Partitioning is only needed when the build side does not fit. With S in memory the join can build once and stream R past it.

options.text: It falls from about 3 transfers per page to about 1, because nothing is written out and read back
options.explanation: Correct. Grace hash reads, writes and rereads every page: about 7,200 page I/Os. With S in memory, each table is read once: about 2,400.

options.text: It halves, because only S stops being partitioned while R is still written out
options.explanation: Once S is held whole in memory, R has no partitions to be matched against, so it simply streams past the hash table. Neither table is written out.

options.text: It rises, because a bigger hash table must be written to disk
options.explanation: An in-memory hash table is not written to disk at all. Writing to disk is exactly what the extra memory avoids.

workedExample:
Compare what happens to each page:

1. **Grace hash.** Partition both tables: read every page and write it to a partition (2 transfers). Then read every partition once to join it (1 transfer). Three transfers per page of 2,400 pages is about 7,200.
2. **S fits in memory.** Read S once to build the hash table, then read R once and probe. One transfer per page: about 2,400.

That single read of each table is the lower bound for an unindexed join in this model. The extra memory removes the whole write-and-reread round trip, which is why memory budgets such as `work_mem` matter so much for hash joins.
